x: Chemical weathering is the process that breaks down rock through chemical changes. Rainfall and temperature can affect the rate at which rocks weather. High temperatures and greater rainfall increase the rate of chemical weathering. Rocks in tropical regions exposed to abundant rainfall and hot temperatures weather much faster than similar rocks residing in cold, dry regions. Rainwater may contain impurities from the atmosphere in the form of dust particles and dissolved gases like oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. When water (e.g. rainwater) mixes with carbon dioxide gas in the air or in air pockets in soil, a weak acid solution, called carbonic acid, is produced. When carbonic acid flows through the cracks of some rocks, it chemically reacts with the rock causing some of it to dissolve. This process is called carbonation. It is very active in limestone regions. Rainwater contains dissolved oxygen from the atmosphere, which can participate in oxidation processes that contribute to weathering. Oxygen in rainwater reacts with minerals, particularly iron-bearing ones, to form oxides or rust, leading to weakening and breakdown. Hence, both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I. The northern part of the western coastal area is called Konkan Coast (Mumbai and Goa) the central part is called Kanara Coast and the southern part is called Malabar Coast. *The Eastern coastal area has developed as a result of deltas of rivers like Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Hence the Eastern coasts are very fertile. The region of eastern coastal area falling between Mahanadi and Krishna rivers is called Northern Circars. *The Coromandel coast extends from Krishna delta in the state of Andhra Pradesh to Cape Comorin (Kanyakumari) in Tamil Nadu. *The important harbors situated on the western coast are - Mumbai (Maharashtra), Janjira (Maharashtra), Udupi (Karnataka), Kochi (Kerala) and New Mangalore (Karnataka) etc. *The important harbours on the eastern coast are Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Haldia (West Bengal), Paradip (Odisha), Kamarajar (Tamil Nadu) and V.O. Chidambaranar (Tamil Nadu).

x: A stack is an erosional feature, left when a sea arch collapses. Tombolo, bar and spit are depositional ridges of sand or shingle.

x: Stalactites, stalagmites and pillars form when groundwater dissolves limestone and redeposits calcium carbonate in caves. They are therefore karst (underground water) features, not running water, wind or glacial ones.
